title: The Beekeeper's Late Summer Evening
subtitle: A slow sleep story for tonight
about: An invented story about a beekeeper tending her hives on a warm evening at the end of summer. Not a true story.
text:
Welcome. This story is invented, and it is meant to be heard slowly. There is nothing to remember and nothing to solve. If you drift off before the end, that is exactly as it should be, and the story will go on quietly without you.

Let your body sink into the bed. Let your shoulders loosen and your hands lie open. Breathe in slowly through your nose, and let the breath leave your mouth in a long, soft sigh. Once more. In, and out. Good.

Now picture a hillside at the end of summer. It is late August, and the evening has just begun. The grass on the slope has gone gold at the tips, and the air is still warm, like a room where someone has recently been sitting. A single path winds up the hill between the trees.

At the top of the path there is an old orchard. Apple trees stand in loose rows, their branches bent with green and red fruit, and the grass beneath them is long and soft. A few apples have already fallen, and they lie in the shade, giving off a sweet and faintly winey smell.

Among the trees stand twelve white boxes, set on low wooden stands. They are beehives, and they have been here for many summers. The paint on them has faded to the colour of milk, and moss has crept along their feet. A low, steady hum rises from them, like a far-off kettle.

The woman who keeps them is called Hester. She is sixty-eight years old, with a weathered, kind face and grey hair twisted into a knot at the back of her head. She wears a faded blue shirt with the sleeves rolled up, and a wide straw hat that has been mended more than once.

Hester has walked this path every evening for thirty summers. Her boots know every stone on it. She does not need to look down, so she looks up instead, at the sky, which is turning slowly from pale gold to peach, and then to a soft, dusty rose.

She carries a small tin can with a spout, and a wooden box with a handle. The can is her smoker, and the box holds her tools, a flat steel lever, a soft brush made of feathers, and a folded cloth. She sets them down at the edge of the orchard, beside a ring of smooth grey stones.

This is where she makes her little fire. She kneels, and gathers a handful of dry grass, and a few twigs of apple wood that she keeps in a basket under a tree. She builds them into a small tent, and strikes a match, and holds it low, and the flame takes hold without any fuss.

The fire is small and kind. It crackles a little, and then settles into a steady glow. The smoke that rises from it is thin and sweet, and it smells of apples and warm bread. Hester sits back on her heels, and watches the flames for a while, as one watches an old friend.

The bees are coming home. You can see them in the low light, tiny dark specks sliding down through the air. Each one is heavy with pollen, and each flies straight to its own door, lands with a little bump, and walks inside. There is no hurry in any of it, only the plain work of the day, ending.

Hester lights the smoker with a twist of burning grass, and feeds it a pinch of dry leaves. A soft white cloud puffs from its spout. She walks to the first hive, and puffs the smoke gently across the entrance. The humming softens, as though a large, kind hand had been laid over it.

She lifts the lid, slowly, and the smell rises to meet her. It is warm, and sweet, and a little like candle wax, and a little like flowers that have been pressed in a book. She breathes it in, and her shoulders drop, and she smiles, because it is the smell she loves most in the world.

Inside, the frames hang side by side, each one covered with bees. They move in slow patterns, over the golden combs, and they hardly notice her at all. Hester does not lift them out. She only looks, and nods, and says quietly, as she says every night, good evening, ladies.

She goes from hive to hive, and does the same at each. A puff of smoke, a lifted lid, a look, a nod. The rhythm is so gentle that it feels almost like walking in a dream. Every hive has its own sound, a little higher or lower, and she knows them all by ear.

The sun slips behind the far hills, and the sky above the orchard turns the colour of the inside of a shell. A pale moon has risen over the eastern fields, thin as a thumbnail, and the first star is blinking awake just beside it.

Hester pauses beneath the oldest apple tree. Its trunk is twisted and silver, and its branches arch overhead like the roof of a small cathedral. She lays her palm on the bark, and it is still warm from the day, and rough in a comforting way. She stands there for a while, and does nothing.

Somewhere in the long grass, a cricket begins to sing. Then another answers, a little further off. Soon there are dozens of them, a soft, silvery chorus that rises and falls across the hill. It is the sound of a warm night settling into itself.

Hester returns to the fire, and adds one more piece of apple wood. The flames wake up, and lean, and then settle again. She takes a small pan from her box, and a heel of brown bread, wrapped in a cloth, and a jar with a faded label. She has everything she needs.

She slices the bread, and toasts it on a stick over the embers. The crust crackles, and the smell grows warm and golden. Then she opens the jar, and a deep amber honey slides out in a slow, thick ribbon. It catches the firelight, and glows, as though it had swallowed a small piece of the sun.

She spreads the honey on the warm bread, and it melts a little into the crumb. The first bite is sweet, and soft, and tastes of every flower the bees visited this summer. She eats slowly, and gratefully, and does not think about anything except how good it is.

A cup of tea sits beside her on a flat stone, brewed from mint she picked at the edge of the orchard. The steam rises in a lazy curl. She holds the cup in both hands, and feels the warmth spread slowly up her arms, all the way to her shoulders, and her neck, and her jaw.

The fire murmurs. Every so often an ember pops, and a tiny spark floats up into the dark, rising and rising until it is hard to tell it from the stars. Hester watches it go, and thinks that the night is a very large and kind place, with room for sparks and sleepers alike.

After a while, a moth finds the firelight. It is a soft, pale thing, with dusty wings, and it circles the flame once, twice, and then settles on a nearby stone, as if it, too, had decided that this was a good place to rest. Hester does not disturb it.

Behind her, in the shadow of the wall, stands the little honey house. It is no bigger than a garden shed, with a slate roof and a crooked door. Inside, rows of clean jars wait on a wooden shelf, each one with its lid, each one lined up like a small, patient choir. Tomorrow they will be filled. Tonight they only catch the last of the light.

She thinks of the man who taught her all this. He was her neighbour once, an old beekeeper with large, slow hands, who let a girl of thirty carry his tools and ask a hundred questions. He never answered quickly. He would watch the bees for a long time, and then say, look, and she would look, and slowly she learned.

A hedgehog appears at the edge of the firelight. It is a small, round shape with a nose that twitches, and it shuffles through the grass as though it had all the time in the world. It sniffs at a fallen apple, and decides that it will do, and begins, very carefully, to eat. Hester smiles, and stays quite still.

The wind turns, just a little, and the smoke leans toward the trees. A few apple leaves rustle, and settle again. High above, a pair of owls call to each other, one near, one far, in a slow and gentle conversation that has been going on in this valley for longer than anyone can say.

She stretches her legs out in the grass, and tilts her head back to look at the stars. They are coming out now, one by one, then in dozens, then in a great soft scatter across the dark. She does not try to name them. It is enough that they are there, and that they are patient.

When the tea is finished, she washes her cup at the old iron pump behind the orchard wall. The water is cold, and clear, and it runs over her wrists with a clean, bright sound. She dries her hands on her shirt, and breathes in the smell of damp stone and grass.

Beyond the wall stands her little hut. It is a small wooden house on iron wheels, painted green, with a round roof and a tiny chimney. It has been standing in this corner of the orchard for as long as she has kept the bees, and it feels like part of the hill itself.

She climbs the three wooden steps, and the door opens with a soft, familiar creak. Inside, it is snug and warm. There is a narrow bed with a patchwork quilt, a shelf with a few books, a lantern hanging from the ceiling, and a small window that looks out over the hives.

She lights the lantern, and it fills the hut with a low, honey-coloured glow. She hangs her hat on its nail, and sits on the edge of the bed, and unlaces her boots. They come off with a small sigh, and her feet feel light and free against the cool wooden floor.

She opens the window a little, just enough to let the night in. A soft breeze drifts through, carrying the smell of apples, and smoke, and cut grass. Far down the hill, she can hear the hum of the hives, quieter now, a long, slow, sleepy sound.

On the shelf there is a small jar, and in the jar a single sprig of lavender. She takes it down, and holds it to her nose, and breathes in. The scent is clean and gentle. She lays the sprig on her pillow, and it perfumes the whole small room.

On the sill of the window sits a small blue bowl, and in the bowl lies a handful of smooth pebbles she has gathered over the years, one for each summer. She runs a finger over them, and they click softly together. Some are grey, some are white, and one is a pale green she found by the stream.

The hut smells of cedar and old paper and a little of honey. Every board in it has been warmed by the day, and gives back its warmth slowly, the way a good stove does. The quiet in the room is not empty. It is full, like a cup of still water.

She changes into a soft old nightgown that has been washed so many times it feels like a cloud. She folds her shirt over the back of the chair, and sets her boots side by side, and checks, with a glance through the window, that the little fire is still safe within its ring of stones.

It is, of course. It is only a low red glow now, a handful of embers with a thin silver crust of ash. They breathe softly in the dark, brightening, and fading, brightening, and fading, like a very slow heartbeat. By morning they will be cold, and she will not need to do a thing.

Hester slides beneath the quilt. It is heavy and soft and smells faintly of sunshine. She lets her head sink into the pillow, and feels the weight of it leave her neck. The mattress is firm and kind, and it carries her like a quiet boat on a very calm lake.

She turns down the lantern until it is only a small gold bead. Then she lies still, and listens. The crickets sing. The bees hum. Somewhere in the orchard, an apple lets go of its branch, and thumps softly into the grass. And then, once again, there is nothing but the night.

She thinks, without trying to, of the summer that is ending. She thinks of the mornings, bright and cool, and the afternoons, thick with the smell of clover. She thinks of the bees, and how many flowers they have visited, and how they have turned them, one tiny drop at a time, into this gold.

Nothing in her mind is pulling, or pushing, or asking for an answer. Her thoughts drift past like clouds on a windless day, slowly, and without a sound. She watches them go, and does not follow, and each one that passes leaves a little more space behind it.

Outside, the moon climbs higher, and silvers the tops of the apple trees. The white hives glow softly in its light, twelve small lanterns in the grass. A single star slides across the sky, and goes out, and no one is disturbed by it at all.

Hester's breathing slows. In, and then out, a little longer each time. Her hands lie loosely on the quilt, and her fingers feel warm and heavy. The hum of the hives and the song of the crickets blend together, until she cannot tell the one from the other, and does not need to.

Now it is your turn to do just the same. Let your breath find its own pace. Let your arms and your legs grow heavy, as if the bed were holding every part of you. Let your jaw rest, and your brow soften, and your thoughts float away like sparks from a small fire.

Imagine, if you like, that you are lying in that little green hut, with the window open, and the quilt up to your chin. You can hear the bees, humming softly in the dark. Each hum is a small, warm wave, and each wave carries a little more of your day away.

There is nothing left to do. The orchard is looking after itself. The hives are full of sleeping bees, and the fire is a gentle red glow, and the moon is keeping watch over all of it. You are warm, and you are safe, and the whole night is yours to rest in.

Down on the hill, the last cricket falls silent. The grass leans, just once, in a breath of wind. And Hester sleeps, with a sprig of lavender by her cheek, and the smell of honey still in the air, and the long, slow summer dark all around her.

You can rest now.

Goodnight.
